sources.title: Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India, 2024 INSC 113
sources.locator: Lead opinion paras 24, 108, 124–127, 209–219; Annexure I, printed pp 153–157; specifically paras 217–218 on collection after the 2019 interim direction

cases.title: Electoral bonds: the missing collection years
cases.question: Why did the ECI’s recorded collection stop at 2019 despite an interim direction the Court later treated as continuing?
cases.finding: The 2024 judgment records a concrete disagreement over the 2019 disclosure order: ECI counsel described collection confined to 2019, while the Court said the direction continued. The institutional visibility gap deserves reconstruction; its cause and any donor-specific benefit remain unproved.

geography.label: New Delhi / Union institutions
geography.basis: Seat of the legislature, Union ministries and courts concerned; nationwide rule scope, not a payment location.

claims.text: The 2024 Court rejected ECI counsel’s reading that the sealed-cover collection direction ended in 2019.
claims.response: ECI counsel grounded the narrower reading in paragraph 14 of the interim order.
claims.alternative: Ambiguous implementation and record management may explain the gap without coordination.
claims.falsifier: A dated ECI inventory showing complete later submissions would narrow the apparent collection gap.

claims.text: Donation and award proximity alone does not establish quid pro quo.
claims.response: The Court declined the requested SIT on ordinary-remedy grounds; this is not exoneration of every transaction.
claims.alternative: Lawful donation and competitively justified awards can share dates around election and tender calendars.
claims.falsifier: A source-closed donor-beneficiary match, decision deviation and corroborating communications could support a specific allegation.
missingRecords: Original serial-number purchase and redemption files

whatWeKnow: Bond anonymity and removal of the corporate contribution cap were struck down in February 2024.
The Court preserved donor privacy and reducing unaccounted money as argued rationales but found the challenged scheme constitutionally deficient.
The August 2024 order separates constitutional invalidity from transaction-specific criminal allegations.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether submissions existed but were not inventoried, whether later notices were issued, or whether any ministry instructed the narrower collection.
No donor-payment/award dataset was freshly joined in this file.
The 2025 review disposition is secondary-only; subsequent donor-specific proceedings are outside this bounded file.

actors.authority: Administer the scheme and communicate purchase windows.

Ensure effective judicial relief and public information rights.

options.label: Maintain continuing collection and seek clarification
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Dated notices, recurring inventories and a clarification application should exist.

options.label: Treat the deadline as a one-window instruction
options.expectedObservableOutcome: 2019 records with subsequent absence of notices, plus documented interpretive reasoning.

decisionAnalysis.observedOutcome: In 2024 ECI counsel reported collection only for 2019; the Court rejected the narrow interpretation and required later bank disclosures.
hindsightLimits: Retrospective reconstruction using a 2024 account of 2019 events, not an archived ex-ante information set.
The counterfactual options are oversight analysis, not a finding that an actor chose concealment.

hypothesis.proposition: A discontinuity in ECI’s collection after the 2019 bond window may have delayed scrutiny of donor-recipient links; deliberate inter-agency weakening is one unproved explanation that must be separated from interpretation and recordkeeping failures.
hypothesis.assessmentReason: A disputed collection gap is recorded, but evidence of instruction, agreement, donor benefit or suppressed records was not obtained.
hypothesis.jurisdiction: Union electoral-finance legislation and ECI compliance with Supreme Court directions; state contract authorities are not presumed involved.

rules.operativePeriod: 2019-04-12 onward as construed by the Court

rules.requirement: 2017 removed the former 7.5% average-profit corporate cap and party-name disclosure; the Court invalidated those changes and anonymity.

alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Dated instructions, objections, receipt inventory and legal advice.

alternatives.discriminatingRecord: Contemporaneous legal note, notices and requests for clarification.

cases.title: FCRA: did retroactive reclassification close the files?
cases.question: Which historical donor receipts were reassessed after the 2016 and 2018 amendments, under what eligibility test, and with what reasoned outcome?
cases.period: Pre-2010 donation baseline; 2014 judgment; 2016–2018 amendments; status check October 2026
cases.finding: The amendments changed the foreign-source test and extended it back to 1976 after the 2014 reappraisal direction concerning BJP and Congress receipts. The missing link is the donor-specific administrative application: neither closure orders nor a full FEMA eligibility assessment were obtained.

geography.label: New Delhi / Union institutions
geography.basis: Seat of the legislature, Union ministries and courts concerned; nationwide rule scope, not a payment location.

claims.text: Finance Act 2018 section 220 extended the 2016 proviso’s deemed insertion date to 5 August 1976.
claims.response: MHA’s contemporaneous explanation was harmonisation with FDI policy and corporate/CSR law.
claims.alternative: A generally applicable legal clarification can benefit previously challenged recipients without proving a bargain.
claims.falsifier: Different enacted text or a later controlling judgment changing this interpretation would require revision.

claims.text: ADR alleges the retrospective change was intended to protect BJP and Congress from the earlier judgment.
claims.response: MHA stated a policy-consistency purpose. The 2014 Court used prima-facie language and directed action; it did not enter a criminal conviction.
claims.alternative: The broader legal rule could have been applied to all eligible companies for a policy reason.
claims.falsifier: Reasoned files demonstrating uniform application and unrelated rationale would weaken the selective-relief hypothesis.
missingRecords: Reappraisal/closure orders for both parties and comparator donors

whatWeKnow: The two enacted amendment texts are retained from MHA scans.
The 2014 judicial baseline concerns donations up to 2009 and precedes the Modi Union administration.
The Court recorded historical majority shareholding of Sterlite and Sesa by UK-incorporated Vedanta; founder nationality did not erase the then foreign-source classification.
Both BJP and Congress appear in the historical dispute; the inquiry is not limited to the governing party.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Which receipts satisfied the new foreign-investment limits at their contribution dates.
Whether particular reappraisal files were closed, continued or resolved on an independent basis.
The petitioner’s hearing lead is stale; the current final merits disposition of the amendment challenge has not been verified.

nextRecords.holder: Donor companies, RBI and competent ministry
nextRecords.purpose: Test eligibility rather than assuming every foreign-controlled donor qualified.

cases.title: Who selects the election overseer?
cases.question: Does the 2023 selection design constrain independent oversight in actual decisions, or do transparent selection, tenure and judicial checks preserve it?
cases.finding: Two of the three statutory selection seats belong to the PM and a PM-nominated minister, but formal composition does not prove how anyone voted or how an appointee acted. The September 2026 joint order concerns bench constitution, with later recall activity reported; constitutional merits remain unestablished in the records inspected.

geography.label: New Delhi / Union institutions
geography.basis: Seat of the legislature, Union ministries and courts concerned; nationwide rule scope, not a payment location.

claims.text: Section 7 places the PM, opposition leader and a PM-nominated Cabinet minister on the selection committee.
claims.response: The Union defended legislative authority and institutional separation; statutory transparency, tenure and removal protections must also be considered.
claims.alternative: A politically appointed official can still make independent decisions under legal duties and protected tenure.
claims.falsifier: A complete selection and decision record showing substantive scrutiny and even-handed outcomes would weaken an operational-capture hypothesis.

claims.text: The 23 September 2026 opinions did not finally uphold or invalidate the challenged appointment mechanism.
claims.response: Judges differed on reference; their joint direction placed the papers before the CJI. Later recall activity is secondary-only here.
claims.alternative: Procedural disagreement is normal judicial process, not evidence of coordination or bias.
claims.falsifier: A later signed final merits judgment or recall disposition would update this procedural account.
missingRecords: Constitution Bench listing and final disposition

whatWeKnow: The passed Bill and final reproduced Act contain an explicit transparency duty for selection procedure.
No-reappointment and removal protections provide competing institutional safeguards.
The split opinions differ over the need for a larger bench; the joint order controls the procedural outcome.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Actual selector votes, private conversations, candidate scoring or how those affected later ECI decisions.
Whether any specified electoral-finance or enforcement decision changed because of this selection design.

actors.authority: Debate and pass the proposed selection design; this is the Bill-stage decision, before statutory selector powers commenced.
actors.incentive: Institutional choices concerning democratic accountability, independence and an administrable appointment process; no private motive inferred.

actors.authority: Sponsor and administer the proposed appointment framework; future Search Committee role is prospective at this decision date.
actors.incentive: Create an operative statutory process with qualifications, transparency and service protections.

informationThen.text: The prior Anoop Baranwal mechanism was interim until Parliament legislated, as the later court opinions explain; it was not a permanent command to copy its exact composition.
The passed Bill already contained the proposed composition and transparency duty on 12 December 2023.

options.label: Executive-majority committee with documented scrutiny
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Detailed criteria, deliberation and protected-tenure decisions permit assessment of independence despite appointment origins.

options.label: A design with an independent selector
options.expectedObservableOutcome: Different selector composition could reduce aligned preferences but would still require competence, transparency and outcome checks.

decisionAnalysis.observedOutcome: The statute adopted PM/opposition/minister composition. In September 2026 the Court was still addressing reference procedure; later recall mentioning was reported in October.
hindsightLimits: This compares institutional options, not a claim that a particular official acts on a private command.
No payoff matrix, equilibrium, causal estimate or predictive calibration is claimed.
PM, opposition leader and minister selection powers are later statutory roles; they are not treated as powers already exercised on the Bill passage date.

hypothesis.proposition: An executive-majority selection design may reduce the independence of later electoral oversight if nomination preferences are transmitted into decisions; that causal link requires actual selection and decision evidence beyond the statutory seat count.
hypothesis.assessmentReason: The institutional channel exists in law; transmission into a particular partisan oversight outcome was not established.
hypothesis.jurisdiction: Union appointment legislation under Article 324, statutory selection committee and ECI; not state election commissions or a claim of PM power over every local electoral act.

tests.question: Were candidate evaluation and dissent meaningful under the transparency duty?

tests.question: Does executive selection establish actual capture of ECI decisions?

tests.expectedIfAlternative: Mixed decisions and consistent reasons remain after controlling case composition and legal changes.
tests.observation: No such causal outcome dataset was built here; separate judicial opinions and a procedural order cannot substitute for it.

proposedLinks.question: Is there documented transmission from selector preferences to a specific ECI oversight decision?

Separate opinions and joint procedural order on larger-bench consideration.

hypothesis.comparison: Before/after comparisons must include pre-2023 executive appointments, the short interim committee period, all comparable decisions and both favourable/adverse outcomes. Do not select only disputed rolls or only one party’s complaints.
inferenceLimits: Retrospective reconstruction, not a preregistered prediction.
A statutory nomination role is not a corrupt relationship.
The reported recall issue is not published as a personal-bias finding or a family influence edge.
